studies.title: The Cave And The Ornament
studies.meaning: The surah opens with praise for a Book that has no crookedness in it, straight and confirming, sent to warn and to give good news. Then two hard sentences: the messenger is told he may destroy himself with grief over people who will not believe, and the world is described as an ornament placed on the earth to test which of them acts best, before being stripped to bare ground. Then the youths in the cave appear, introduced as something less remarkable than the reader assumes.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Classical sources report with broad agreement that the Meccan leadership sent to the scholars of Medina for questions to test the message, and were given three: the sleepers in the cave, a traveller who reached the ends of the earth, and the spirit. This surah answers the first two and the third comes at the end of the preceding surah. The reports differ on details but agree on the shape.

keyTerms.note: A word for a bend in something that should be straight, used of a stick or a road. Denying it of the Book at the very first ayah sets up the surah, which is about things that look bent until explained.
Decoration added to a thing rather than belonging to it, like jewellery on a person. Applied to everything on earth, it makes the world's attraction real and also removable, which the next ayah does.
A rare and violent word for killing yourself by grief or effort, used of an animal driven past exhaustion. It measures how heavily the refusal of others was being felt.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Caves were shelter of the last resort in that landscape: cool, defensible, and used by shepherds, fugitives and travellers caught out after dark. Everyone knew one. The story the surah is about to tell concerned young men who took refuge from a ruler in exactly such a place, so the setting needed no explaining. What needed explaining was why God would find it unremarkable.
studies.didYouKnow: The surah's opening ayat contain a rare pause mark in the standard printed text, placed after the word for crookedness, which prevents a reciter from joining it to the word that follows and reversing the sense. It is one of only a handful of such marks in the whole Quran. Reciting this surah on Fridays is a long-established practice.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The seventh ayah sets the terms for everything the surah will narrate. The world's attractiveness is not an illusion and not a trap; it is described as a deliberate arrangement whose purpose is to find out which of them is best in conduct. That makes ordinary life the examination rather than a distraction from it. The eighth ayah then removes the ornament, which places the test inside a frame the person taking it can see.

crossReferences.why: Names the same purpose for death and life: to test which of you is best in deed.
Returns to the same image later in the surah, water and then wealth as ornament.
Uses a similar phrase about grieving yourself to death over those who will not believe.

studies.applyIt: Look at one thing in your home you saved for and now barely see. Not to feel guilty about it: just register that the wanting was more vivid than the having. The surah calls the world an ornament and means it as a description of how attraction works, not as a warning against owning things. Notice the pattern once and it stays noticeable.

studies.title: Sealed Ears And A Counted Sleep
studies.meaning: Three short ayat compress years into a sentence. God seals the young men's hearing in the cave, an idiom the commentators read as a sleep no sound could interrupt. Then He raises them, and the stated purpose is that two disputing groups would learn which had reckoned the span better. Only after that does the Quran say it is now giving the account in truth, and it names them plainly: young men who believed, and were then increased in guidance.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The classical biographies report that leaders in Mecca gathered questions designed to test the claim of the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him), and that the story of young men who vanished long ago was among them. Whether or not a reader accepts that report, the surah clearly addresses an audience that already knew some version of the tale and disagreed about its details.

keyTerms.note: A plural used of youths in their strength. Arabic usage carries more than age, adding readiness and a willingness to stand up for something, which suits people who moved first while their society stayed still.
A stretch of time with an end point, unlike an open-ended duration. The word frames the sleep as a period that can in principle be counted, which is why the dispute about its length becomes possible.

Placed after their believing rather than before it. The commentators read the order closely: guidance here comes as an increase given to those who have already turned, so it reads as reward rather than as cause.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Caves in the hills were ordinary shelter, not mystery. Shepherds waited out midday heat in them, travellers slept in them, and a fugitive could disappear into one for as long as the water held. Along the caravan road north to Syria, stories of people who had vanished into the hills circulated among traders and were retold with different numbers and different endings at every stop.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for cave occurs six times in the Quran, and every one of them falls inside this surah, which takes its name from it. The companion word in the surah's opening, naming whatever was inscribed alongside them, occurs exactly once in the whole Book. That scarcity is part of why commentators differ so widely over what it means.
studies.theologicalSignificance: God is made the narrator, and the passage marks the difference between a tale that circulates and an account given in truth. The stated reason for the waking concerns human knowledge rather than divine: two parties find out what neither could calculate. And guidance appears as something increased over time, a continuing supply rather than a single gift handed over once.

crossReferences.why: The prayer the youths make on entering the cave, which these ayat answer with sleep and with guidance.
Another cave used as shelter, where a hunted pair are told not to grieve because God is with them.
Gives the number of years, which is what the two disputing groups here were trying to settle.

studies.applyIt: Notice where this passage puts guidance: after the choice, not before it. Pick one thing you already believe is right and do it once today without waiting to feel more certain first. The increase described here is not promised to people who are waiting for clarity. It is described as arriving after a step is taken.

studies.title: We Tied Their Hearts Together
studies.meaning: The ayah gives the cause before the act. God bound their hearts, and only then did they stand and speak. Their statement is short and total: our Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth, and we will call on no god besides Him. They close by naming what the alternative would be, an outrage, a wild departure from the truth. The courage is presented as something supplied, not summoned.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in a period when a small number of believers were declaring themselves against the settled religion of their city and paying for it. The commentators note that the surah's four stories all turn on holding a position under pressure. The young men in the cave are not given names, dates or a country, which keeps the pattern visible rather than the particular history.

keyTerms.note: From tying an animal so it cannot bolt. The image is of a heart secured against panic rather than a heart made brave, which is why the same root is used for stationing horses at a frontier.
A physical standing that Arabic also uses for taking a public stand. Both senses are live here, since what follows is a declaration made where it could be heard and answered.
From a root meaning to go far beyond the limit. It describes a statement so far off that it is not merely wrong but extravagant, which is how they classify the claim they refuse to make.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Religion in Arabian towns was inherited and public. A household kept its idols, a tribe kept its shrine, and a young man's standing came from his family's place in that order. To say aloud that the gods your father served were nothing was not a private opinion; it withdrew you from the protection network that fed you, married you and buried you. Young men had the least standing to lose and the most to risk.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb translated here as strengthening is literally a word for tying something down, and the Quran uses the same root elsewhere for the steadying of a mother's heart and for horses kept ready at a border post. The connecting thread is not emotion but restraint: something is held in place so that it cannot run.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Steadiness is attributed to God before the human act is described, which cuts against reading faith as raw willpower. Yet the men still stand and still speak, so the divine act does not replace theirs. The passage also shows a creed stated by its scope, the heavens and the earth, before it is stated by its exclusions, which keeps the refusal grounded in something positive.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same image of a heart bound fast, there of the mother of Moses when she nearly spoke.
God binds hearts and steadies feet before a battle, the same verb applied to a community under fear.
Continues their speech, moving from what they affirm to the challenge they put to their people.

studies.applyIt: Think of a moment when you held steady and felt afterwards that you had barely managed it. This ayah suggests the steadiness was given before you noticed needing it. Before your next difficult conversation, ask for that rather than for the right words. Then have the conversation anyway, because the standing here is still theirs to do.

studies.title: Why Bring No Clear Proof
studies.meaning: The young men turn from stating their own position to examining their people's. They do not mock the idols; they ask for evidence, and note that none is offered. Then the argument widens into a question with no answer: who does greater wrong than someone who invents a lie and attributes it to God. The commentators observe that the case is made entirely on the ground of proof, which is why it can be repeated by anyone in any century.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The Quran's early argument with the city was rarely about ritual and often about warrant: the objects worshipped had no case behind them and no revelation supporting them. Putting this reasoning into the mouths of young men from a distant past shows the audience their own dispute already being conducted, and won, long before their grandfathers were born.

keyTerms.note: The word means power, and it means the kind of evidence that gives an argument power. Arabic keeps both senses in one term, so demanding proof and denying authority are here the same move.
Used of cutting and stitching something together. The image is of a claim assembled rather than received, which is exactly the charge: these gods were made, and so were the stories told about them.

From a root for putting something out of its proper place as much as for cruelty. Attributing a lie to God is wrong in that structural sense, taking what belongs in one place and setting it in another.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabian argument was oral, public and adversarial. Disputes over lineage, water rights and honour were settled by producing witnesses and evidence in front of an audience that judged on the spot. Demanding clear authority for a claim was a familiar move at a well or in a market, and the phrasing here borrows that courtroom instinct and turns it toward the objects the town had never thought to question.
studies.didYouKnow: The question form used here, asking who does greater wrong than a particular person, recurs more than a dozen times across the Quran, each time filled with a different offence. It is never answered. The construction leaves the comparison open so that the listener supplies the verdict rather than receiving it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage sets the standard of religious truth at evidence rather than inheritance, and it applies that standard first to the speakers' own community. It also names the worst wrong as a speech act, saying about God what God did not say. That places falsehood about the divine above other offences, because it corrupts the source everything else is measured against.

crossReferences.why: Demands the same thing of the Meccans directly, asking for their proof and pointing them to the Book.
Uses the identical question form about inventing lies against God, with no answer supplied.
Says the names of the idols were given by ancestors, with no authority sent down for them.

studies.applyIt: Take one religious claim you repeat because you grew up hearing it, and spend ten minutes finding out where it actually comes from. Not to doubt it, but to know. The young men here did not reject their inheritance blindly; they asked what it rested on and found nothing. Knowing the ground under your own position is the same work.

studies.title: Take Shelter And Mercy Unfolds
studies.meaning: Someone among them speaks, and the advice is practical: you have already separated from them, so go to the cave. What follows is not a guarantee of rescue but two promises of a different order. Your Lord will spread out some of His mercy over you, and He will arrange ease in your affair. The commentators note the partitive phrasing, some of His mercy, and read it as deliberate restraint rather than a small offer.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah was heard by people who had already begun leaving, some to Abyssinia, some into hiding within the city. Withdrawal from a hostile majority was a live question, not a metaphor, and this ayah presents it as a legitimate step rather than a failure of nerve. The classical commentators do not fix a country or a century for the young men.

keyTerms.note: A reflexive form meaning to set yourself apart. It describes distance taken deliberately, not exile imposed, and the Quran uses the same root for a father stepping away from his household's worship.
The verb for an animal returning to its den or a traveller reaching lodging at nightfall. It carries arrival and rest rather than flight, which changes the tone of the instruction.
From a root for gentleness and for the elbow, the joint that lets an arm bend. What is promised is not removal of difficulty but the give that makes a hard thing workable.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Withdrawal had a recognised shape in Arabia. A man in a blood dispute could leave the settlement and live rough until tempers cooled or terms were agreed. Hill country near the towns held caves with a spring nearby, and people knew which ones held water through summer. Choosing a cave was a practical calculation about heat, water and how far a search party would bother to walk.
studies.didYouKnow: The promise here is partitive: God will spread out for you some of His mercy, not His mercy. The same construction appears in the Quran wherever a specific portion is being granted rather than the whole attribute, and classical commentators treated the small particle as carrying real weight rather than as ornament.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage licenses retreat without calling it defeat, and it defines the divine response in terms of provision and workability rather than deliverance. Mercy is described as spread out, an act with extent, and ease is described as arranged, an act with design. Both are stated in the future, so the young men enter the cave with a promise but no timetable.

crossReferences.why: Abraham withdraws from his people and from what they call on, using the same root for separation.
Makes the same point about ease arriving with hardship rather than only after it.
The youths had already asked for mercy and for their affair to be set right; this is the answer.

studies.applyIt: There is a situation you keep entering because leaving feels like giving up. Consider that this passage treats stepping away as the sound move, and attaches the promise to the step. Withdraw from one draining conversation this week, without announcing it and without a speech. Then notice what becomes easier in the space that opens.

studies.title: The Sun Leaning Away
studies.meaning: The scene is described as if you were watching. Sunlight swings clear of the cave mouth at both ends of the day, and the sleepers lie in an open space inside, out of the heat and never in shadowless dark. The Quran then names what has been shown: this is among God's signs. The closing sentence widens abruptly from a cave to a principle about guidance, and about the friend a misguided person will not find.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Much of the surrounding surah answers people demanding a wonder as proof. Here the wonder is deliberately undramatic, an arrangement of light and shade over many years, and the commentators read the transition to guidance at the end as the point of the description rather than an appendix to it.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to incline or turn toward, used here in a form that turns it away. The verb suggests a courteous swerve, as though the light were declining to enter rather than being blocked.
A gap or a wide place, occurring only here in the Quran. It marks the sleepers as lying in the roomy part of the cave, ventilated and clear, rather than pressed into a crevice.
From a root for soundness of judgement and knowing the way. The word describes a guide who gets you there, so its absence at the end of the ayah is the loss of direction, not of company.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Anyone who travelled the Hijaz knew how a cave's aspect decided whether it was liveable. A mouth facing the wrong way took the full afternoon sun and became an oven; a mouth angled north stayed cool and dry through summer. Herders chose shelters by that reckoning without thinking about it, so the description here reads to its first audience as a practical detail, precisely observed.
studies.didYouKnow: The word describing the open space where they lay occurs nowhere else in the Quran. The same is true of several words in this narrative, including the threshold where the dog lies and the silver coin sent to the town, giving the story of the cave an unusually high concentration of terms used only once in the entire Book.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A sign is defined here as something ordinary that has been arranged, which shifts the burden from spectacle to attention. The closing lines then place guidance entirely with God while leaving the human act of turning intact elsewhere in the surah. The pairing suggests that noticing the sign and being guided are the same event seen from two sides.

crossReferences.why: Continues the same observed scene, adding the turning of the sleepers and the dog at the entrance.
Lists ordinary regularities of sky, sea and wind as signs for people who use their minds.
States the same limit on guidance, that it does not lie in the hands of even a beloved messenger.

studies.applyIt: Go outside near sunset and watch how the light falls on one wall you pass every day. Give it two minutes without your phone. The wonder in this ayah is not that the sun moved strangely but that someone was paying enough attention to record where it fell. That kind of noticing is a skill, and it is trainable.

studies.title: You Would Think Them Awake
studies.meaning: The description keeps the sleepers between two states. Their eyes give the impression of wakefulness while they sleep; they are turned side to side over the years so the body does not fail; the dog lies with its forelegs stretched at the entrance. Then the perspective shifts to you, the onlooker, who would have fled in terror. The commentators differ over what would have caused the fear, and none of the readings makes it the sleepers' doing.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in a surah addressed to people who denied that a body long in the ground could be raised. The image of preserved sleepers answers that objection sideways rather than head on. The classical sources place the young men in a Christian or pre-Christian setting under a persecuting ruler, but they do not agree on the country, the ruler or the century.

keyTerms.note: A plural adjective for those who are alert, from the root used for waking someone. Setting it directly against the word for sleepers gives the ayah its uncanny effect in a single phrase.
An intensive form suggesting repeated turning. God is named as the one doing it, which is why the detail reads as care rather than as an incidental fact about long sleep.
A word for the entrance or courtyard of a dwelling, occurring only here in the Quran. Using a household term for a cave mouth quietly turns the shelter into a home with a door being watched.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A dog stretched at the threshold was the ordinary sight of a guarded household or camp. Dogs were working animals in Arabia, kept for herding and for warning, and they slept where the entrance was. Anyone hearing this would picture a place that was occupied and defended, not abandoned, which is exactly the impression that would make a passer-by back away.
studies.didYouKnow: The dog of the cave is mentioned in only two ayat of the Quran, yet it appears three separate times inside the single ayah about the sleepers' number, once with each of the three counts people proposed. The animal survives in the story precisely because the guessers kept counting it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Preservation over centuries is presented without any suggestion that the sleepers were doing something. Everything active in the scene is attributed to God, down to the turning of a shoulder. For an audience arguing that resurrection is impossible, the passage answers by showing continuity maintained inside time, which asks less than raising the dead and is still beyond anyone present.

crossReferences.why: A man is kept a hundred years and shown that his food and drink did not spoil.
Returns to this scene from outside, reporting how later generations argued over what was in the cave.
Answers the same objection about bodies reduced to bone by pointing at the first creation.

studies.applyIt: Notice the small verb in the middle of this ayah: they were turned, so that lying still for years did not ruin them. Someone has been doing that for you in ways you have not catalogued. Before you sleep tonight, name one thing that kept working today without your attention, and say thank you for that one thing specifically.

studies.title: A Day, Or Part Of A Day
studies.meaning: They wake and immediately misjudge the time, then hand the question over: your Lord knows best how long you stayed. What follows is startlingly practical. Send one of you to town with this silver, let him look for the best food, let him bring provision, and let him be careful and let nobody notice you. Three centuries have passed and their first concern is lunch, bought discreetly, with money that no longer spends.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah repeatedly measures human estimates of time against God's knowledge, and this is its clearest instance. The classical commentators treat the exchange as reported speech rather than as a scene requiring a date or a place, and they do not settle which city the messenger walked into or which ruler was on the throne when he arrived.

keyTerms.note: A specific word for minted silver rather than wealth in general, occurring only here in the Quran. The precision matters to the story, since coins carry a ruler's face and a date and are what gives the sleepers away.
From a root joining growth and purity, used elsewhere of purified wealth and of a purified soul. Applied to food it asks for what is clean and good rather than for what is cheapest or most plentiful.
A single verb covering tact, softness and care in handling. It occurs nowhere else in the Quran, and copyists have long marked it for its place in the middle of the text.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Buying food in a seventh-century market meant being seen. A stranger's accent, dress and coin were all read at once, and an unfamiliar coin was examined closely because towns knew their own minting. Traders in Mecca handled Byzantine and Persian silver daily and could date a piece by sight. The instruction to be discreet was sound advice that the story then shows failing anyway.
studies.didYouKnow: An old scribal tradition marks the word in this ayah meaning let him be gentle as the midpoint of the Quran counted by letters, and many printed copies still note it in the margin. Modern counts vary with orthography and place the midpoint elsewhere, but the marking has been copied by hand for centuries.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The sleepers' confident wrong answer, corrected by one of their own, models a small piece of religious honesty: say what you know, then hand the rest over. The passage also refuses to let a miracle dissolve ordinary life. People who have just been preserved for three hundred years are still hungry, still cautious, and still required to go and buy something to eat.

crossReferences.why: Supplies the answer they could not give, three hundred years and nine more.
The same question of how long, asked of a man kept a century, with the same corrected estimate.
On the Day of Resurrection people will again misjudge the interval, saying they lingered only ten, or only a day.

studies.applyIt: Practise the sentence they used when the group disagreed: your Lord knows best. Say it once today, out loud, at the moment you would normally defend a guess you are not sure of. Then do what they did next and turn to the practical thing in front of you. Uncertainty about the large question did not stop them eating.

studies.title: If They Discover You
studies.meaning: The speech continues, and this is the reason behind the caution. Two outcomes are named, and they are placed side by side as if they were comparable: stoning, or being forced back into the old religion. The second is treated as the graver danger, since the sentence ends with never being saved. The commentators note that the young men fear apostasy under duress more than they fear execution, which is what the ordering of the two is doing.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, spoken to a community in which believers were being pressed, some to the point of publicly recanting to save themselves. The surah's audience knew what coercion looked like from close range. The story's ruler and city are left unnamed in the Quran, and classical commentators drawing on earlier traditions supply various identifications that they themselves report with caution.

keyTerms.note: From a root for the back and for appearing, giving both discovery and dominance. The verb carries the sense of coming out on top of someone, so being found and being overpowered are one motion.

A word for a community's whole way, its beliefs and the practice that goes with them, rather than for private conviction. Being returned to it means resuming a public life, not just changing an opinion.
From a root meaning to split open the ground for planting. Success in this word is agricultural: breaking through to what was buried, with the harvest arriving long after the labour.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Stoning by a crowd was the punishment a town used when it wanted no single executioner and no blood feud afterwards. Everyone shared the act, so no family could be held responsible. In tribal Arabia that mattered, because a killing normally carried a debt. Being stoned meant dying without the protection of anyone being answerable for it, which is why the threat was so effective.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for success used here gave its name to the call heard from minarets, where the summons is to come to what makes you prosper. Its root sense is the ploughman's work of splitting soil, so the word carries an image of hard opening rather than of easy winning.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage assumes that faith held under threat can be lost from the outside, and it takes that risk seriously rather than promising that sincerity is untouchable. It also ranks the dangers honestly: physical harm is named first and briefly, coercion into the old life is named second and given the fuller consequence. Fear is treated as information here, not as a failing.

crossReferences.why: Addresses the case of someone compelled to recant while the heart remains at rest in faith.
Tells of believers killed rather than turned, with the persecutors named only by their trench.
Shows how the discovery they feared actually came, and what the town made of it.

studies.applyIt: Name the pressure you are actually under, in one sentence, without softening it. These young men said the danger aloud to each other before deciding what to do. Naming it did not make them turn back; it let them plan the errand carefully. Say yours to one person you trust this week, plainly, and then decide.

studies.title: So That They Would Know
studies.meaning: The discovery the sleepers feared is revealed as arranged, and the purpose is stated: so that people would know God's promise is true and the Hour beyond doubt. The town then argues about what to do with the site. One group wants a building over them; another prevails and wants a place of worship. The Quran reports the dispute without endorsing either side, and interrupts it with a single sentence: their Lord knows best about them.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah is answering people who accepted a Creator and denied a resurrection, and this ayah supplies a case in which a long interruption of ordinary life ended in waking. The classical commentators place the discovery in a later, believing generation, but the Quran gives neither date nor location and they follow it in leaving both open.

keyTerms.gloss: We caused them to be found
keyTerms.note: A causative from stumbling. God is named as the one who made people trip over the sleepers, so the discovery is neither accident nor detective work but something arranged to look accidental.
The Quran's usual name for the end of the world, a term for a short interval rather than an age. The choice stresses suddenness and brevity, not the scale of what happens.
A reciprocal form from a root meaning to pull. The picture is of parties tugging a matter in opposite directions, each trying to take it, which fits a quarrel over a shrine.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A holy site in late antiquity was an asset. Pilgrims brought trade, and a town with a shrine had standing among its neighbours and revenue at its gates. Mecca itself lived by exactly this arrangement. An audience there would have recognised the argument over the cave immediately, including the speed with which a wonder becomes a building project.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase saying that the Lord knows best occurs four times inside this one narrative. Once it is on the sleepers' own lips, correcting their guess about how long they had been there. The other three cut across other people's confidence: about who the sleepers were, about how many, and about the length of the stay.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A sign is shown to have a purpose beyond its own strangeness: it is given so that a claim about the future can be believed. The passage also demonstrates how quickly people convert an event into a monument and a monument into a dispute, and it withholds approval from the outcome while reporting it accurately. Knowledge stays with God even where the building goes up.

crossReferences.why: Continues the pattern, listing the numbers people guessed and returning the matter to God's knowledge.
Another long interruption ended by waking, given explicitly as a sign about the raising of the dead.
States plainly that the Hour is coming without doubt and that God will raise those in the graves.

studies.applyIt: Watch for the moment a real experience turns into a thing you manage: a photograph, a plan, a story you tell well. That is what the town did with the cave. Next time something moves you, wait a full day before you do anything with it. See what remains once the impulse to build something has passed.

studies.title: Guessing At The Unknown
studies.meaning: Three counts are quoted, each adding the dog. The Quran labels the first two with a phrase meaning throwing stones at the dark, and pointedly does not label the third, which many commentators take as a quiet signal without treating it as settled. The instruction that follows is about conduct, not arithmetic: say your Lord knows their number, do not argue beyond what is plain, and do not ask any of them for a verdict.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The number of the sleepers was evidently a live disagreement among communities who had inherited the story, and the ayah addresses the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) about how to handle a dispute he had no need to enter. The Quran gives the number of years elsewhere in the surah but never the number of people, and the commentators respect that silence.

keyTerms.note: Literally pelting with stones, used for speaking at random about what cannot be seen. The image is of throwing into darkness and claiming a hit, which is a precise description of confident speculation.
From a root for stroking an udder to draw out the last milk. Arabic uses it for the kind of argument that keeps working a point after everything useful has already been said.
To ask an authority for a considered ruling on a question. The instruction is not to consult anyone on this particular matter, which places the detail outside the range of things worth adjudicating.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Stories crossed Arabia by caravan and grew as they went. A tale picked up in Syria arrived in Mecca months later with new names, rounder numbers and a sharper ending, and the person who told it best was believed. In a culture with no written archive, the authority of a version rested on the confidence of its teller, which is the habit this ayah interrupts.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran gives the length of the sleep exactly, three hundred years and nine more, but never gives the number of sleepers. It quotes three counts and endorses none. The word it uses for that guessing, a noun meaning a stone thrown, appears in this sense only here in the entire Book.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage draws a line between what revelation is for and what it is not. A detail can be true, known to God, and still not worth pursuing, and pursuing it is treated as a failure of proportion rather than of piety. It also models restraint in argument as a religious act, limiting dispute to what is evident and refusing to seek authorities on the rest.

crossReferences.why: Forbids pursuing what you have no knowledge of, since hearing, sight and heart are all questioned.
Repeats the same move about the length of their stay, returning the unknown to God.
Says conjecture avails nothing against the truth, of people who speak confidently about angels.

studies.applyIt: Find the argument you are having, online or at home, that would change nothing if you won it. This ayah's advice is not to argue better but to stop at what is obvious and decline to escalate. Leave one thread unanswered today. Notice how much of the urge to reply was about the topic and how much was about you.

studies.title: Unless God Wills
studies.meaning: A prohibition on a way of speaking, not on planning. Do not say of anything that you will do it tomorrow, without adding that it is subject to God's will. Then two supports are given: remember your Lord if you forget, which the commentators read either as saying the phrase late or as remembering God generally; and a modest hope that He may guide you nearer to what is right. The third ayah returns to the sleepers and states their number of years.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The classical sources report, with reasonable agreement, that the questions put to test the message went unanswered for a period after a promise to answer the next day, and that these ayat came in connection with that delay. The reports vary in detail. The surah then places the instruction directly before a statement of the sleepers' exact duration, which reads as a quiet demonstration of who knows what.

keyTerms.note: The ordinary word for the next day. Its plainness is the point: the prohibition is not about grand plans but about the smallest and most confident unit of the future a person uses.
The verb covers both losing something from memory and neglecting it. Building an allowance for forgetting into the instruction itself keeps the phrase from becoming a test a person can fail.

A word for maturity of judgement, used of a young person old enough to manage property. It names the good outcome as competence rather than as fortune, which fits a surah full of people learning what they did not understand.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Nothing about tomorrow was reliable. A caravan's arrival depended on weather, raiders and the health of animals; a harvest depended on rain that either came or did not; a person could be well in the morning and dead by evening of a fever nobody could name. Promises were made with hedges built in, and everyone had watched a confident plan collapse. The instruction attached a name to a caution people already felt.
studies.didYouKnow: The number of years is given in an unusual way: three hundred years, and they added nine. Commentators have long noted that three hundred solar years correspond almost exactly to three hundred and nine lunar years, which is the calendar the addressees used. The surah gives the figure and then immediately says to leave the knowledge of it to God.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The instruction is about the grammar of a sentence and reaches something larger. Saying you will do something tomorrow asserts a small ownership of the future, and the correction does not remove the plan; it adds a clause. What that clause does is keep intention and outcome in separate hands, which is what allows a person to plan seriously without being destroyed when the plan fails. The permission to say it late is mercy built into the same instruction.

crossReferences.why: Names what no one knows, including what a soul will earn tomorrow.
Jacob gives his sons practical instructions and then hands the judgement back to God.
Immediately before this, the same surah refuses to settle a disputed number.

studies.applyIt: Say the phrase out loud once today, in English or in Arabic, about something small and near: the appointment this afternoon, the meal you are cooking. Not as a superstition and not as a hedge. Just notice what it does to the sentence, and to you, to attach a condition to something you had assumed was settled.

studies.title: How Perfectly He Sees And Hears
studies.meaning: The length of the sleep is handed back to God, and then the ayah does something unusual. Instead of describing His seeing and hearing, it uses an exclamatory form that has no easy English equivalent, closer to how seeing He is, how hearing. The commentators note the shift in register. The ayah closes by denying that anyone shares His judgement, which turns a point about a disputed number into a statement about who decides anything at all.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The story of the cave had reached Arabia in several versions with different figures attached, and the surah keeps redirecting each disputed detail to God's knowledge rather than adjudicating it. This ayah is the last of those redirections in the narrative, after which the surah turns to instructions for the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) about recitation and company.

keyTerms.note: What is absent from perception, whether hidden by distance, by time or by nature. The word covers the future and the interior of things alike, which is why the sleepers' years fall inside it.

An exclamatory form that looks like a command but functions as astonishment. Arabic uses it to express that a quality is beyond measure, so the English needs a whole phrase where the original has a word.
From a root for restraining and for deciding, the same root behind wisdom and behind a bridle. Judgement in this sense is the authority to settle a matter and hold it settled.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabian disputes ended in front of an arbitrator whose authority both parties had accepted in advance. A respected man, often from a neutral clan, heard the case and gave a decision, and his word closed the matter. Sharing that role was unthinkable; two arbitrators meant no arbitration. The final clause borrows the shape of that institution and says God takes no partner in it.
studies.didYouKnow: The two words for seeing and hearing in this ayah use a grammatical form Arabic reserves for wonder, built to look like an imperative. Classical grammarians discussed it at length precisely because a command addressed to God would be impossible, and they settled on reading it as an expression of amazement.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Perception and authority are joined in a single ayah. God sees and hears without limit, and therefore no one shares His decision, since a judgement can only be as good as the knowledge behind it. The passage also treats the unseen as a possession rather than a mystery. What is hidden from everyone is not hidden in itself; it is simply held by one.

crossReferences.why: Places the keys of the unseen with God alone, down to a leaf that falls unnoticed.
Makes the same move about the sleepers' number, handing a disputed figure back to God.
States that God judges with none to reverse His judgement, using the same root for decision.

studies.applyIt: There is a question about your own life you keep re-answering: why it happened, how long it will last, what it meant. Try saying the first half of this ayah about it, that God knows best how long. Then stop the sentence there without adding your theory. Do that each time the question returns today.

studies.title: No One Can Change His Words
studies.meaning: The instruction is to recite what has been revealed, and two reasons follow. There is no one who can alter God's words, and there is no refuge to be found apart from Him. The commentators read the first as covering both the text itself and the promises it carries, so the reciter is not adjusting a message under pressure. The second closes the door on the alternative, which is negotiating with the people applying the pressure.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, at a point when the leadership of the city was reportedly proposing terms: soften some of this, and we will listen. The classical sources record several such approaches. This ayah comes immediately after a warning against wishing away the poor believers who sit with the Prophet, and it answers the same temptation from a different direction.

keyTerms.note: The verb means to read aloud and also to come after in sequence. Both senses fit a text delivered in order over years, and Arabic keeps them in one word rather than two.
A plural that reaches beyond the recited text to God's decrees and promises. The commentators read it in both senses here, so what cannot be altered is the message and the outcome it announces.
From a root meaning to turn aside, so it names the hollow you turn into when running from something. The word is rare, and it appears only twice in the Quran, both times in a denial.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Poetry and oration in Arabia were composed for an audience and adjusted to it. A poet reading the room dropped a line that offended a patron and sharpened one that flattered him, and this flexibility was a mark of skill. A message that could not be edited for its listeners was strange, and part of the Quran's early claim was that it was not that kind of speech.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for a place of refuge in this ayah appears only twice in the entire Quran, and both occurrences are inside denials that any such place exists apart from God. The term is never once used in the affirmative, so the Book introduces the idea only in order to rule it out.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two kinds of stability are asserted together. The message is stable because no one can rewrite it, and the messenger is stable because there is nowhere else to go. The second is the harder claim, since it removes the option of a compromise position. Taken together they define the reciter's task narrowly: deliver it, unmodified, without looking for an exit.

crossReferences.why: Says the word of the Lord is complete in truth and justice, with no one to change it.
Records a demand for a different Quran, and the reply that it cannot be altered by the messenger.
The ayah immediately after, telling the Prophet where to keep his attention and with whom.

studies.applyIt: Read a short passage of the Quran aloud today rather than silently, even three lines, even badly. This ayah pairs recitation with the fact that the words are not yours to adjust. Reading aloud makes that concrete in a way reading with your eyes does not, because your mouth has to take the sentence as it stands.

studies.title: Stay With Those Who Call
studies.meaning: The instruction is to hold yourself with a particular group, and the verb is the one for patience, so staying is presented as something that requires endurance. Those described are people who call on their Lord at the two ends of the day, wanting His face and nothing else. Then the eyes are addressed again, told not to pass over them in search of the world's glitter. The last clause warns against following someone whose priorities have come apart.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Classical reports connect the ayah with a request from leading men of Quraysh that the poor believers, several of them former slaves, be kept away from the gatherings before they would sit and listen. The reports vary in detail, and the commentators generally accept the substance. The instruction answers by reversing the request: stay with those men, and do not look past them.

keyTerms.note: The verb for patience made transitive, so it is not be patient but restrain yourself and keep yourself in place. It concedes that remaining in that company may take effort.
The word for a face, used in the Quran for God's own self and for what is turned towards. Naming it as the object of desire rules out every secondary motive without listing them.

A rare word for something that has run ahead of itself or been squandered. The commentators read it of a life whose affair has slipped past all measure, so the man is not described as wicked but as unmoored.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Who sat with whom was public information in Mecca and carried real weight. An assembly had an order, and a man of standing did not share a mat with a client or a freed slave without it being noticed and discussed. Several of the earliest believers were exactly such men, bought out of ownership or disowned by their families. The instruction to stay with them was an instruction about seating.
studies.didYouKnow: The same word for the world's ornament used at the start of this surah returns here, now as something the eyes might drift towards. The surah uses it three times in different settings, which is one of the ways it holds together. A very similar instruction appears in an earlier surah, where the reason given is that those people call on their Lord morning and evening.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah locates worth in a practice rather than in a person's standing, and then asks the reader to organise his attention accordingly. What makes the group worth staying with is named precisely: they call on their Lord, at both ends of the day, wanting nothing but Him. Nothing is said about their learning, their manners or their usefulness. And the warning at the end is not about a bad man but about a heart made heedless, which is a condition rather than a verdict.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same instruction in almost the same words, with a warning against driving them away.
A whole passage correcting attention given to the influential over a blind man who came seeking.
Repeats the instruction about the eyes and adds the same command about the wing.

studies.applyIt: Think about who you would text if something good happened this week, and who you would text if something bad did. If the two lists are different, notice why. Then this week arrange to spend an hour with someone from the second list who has nothing to offer you except that you are better around them. That is what this ayah is describing.

studies.title: No Reward Is Wasted
studies.meaning: A guarantee stated with an odd grammatical doubling: the sentence begins with those who believe and act well, then restarts and finishes with a different phrase, whoever does good work. The commentators note that the shift widens the promise beyond the group first named. What is promised is negative in form. Nothing is said about the size of the reward, only that none of it is lost, which answers a specific fear about effort that goes unseen.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The ayah follows a hard passage that leaves belief to the hearer's choice and describes the consequence of refusing, and it precedes the parable of two men and their gardens. The commentators report no specific occasion. In Mecca the believers were losing money, work and standing, and much of what they did could not be seen by anyone, which is the situation this sentence addresses.

keyTerms.note: The verb is used of property lost through neglect and of a child left uncared for. Denying it of God frames the reward as something held in safekeeping rather than merely owed.

The phrase is about quality of execution, not quantity. It is the same expression used earlier in this surah for what the test of the world is designed to reveal, which ties the promise back to the purpose.
An ordinary word for a labourer's pay rather than a gift. Using it places the relation in the vocabulary of work done and wages due, which is why the fear of loss makes sense in the first place.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Day labour in that economy was paid at the end of the day and depended entirely on the employer's honesty. A hired man on a harvest or a well had no contract and no court; if the owner denied the work, that was the end of it. Everyone had either been cheated or knew someone who had. A promise from an employer who does not forget was heard against that background.
studies.didYouKnow: The ayah opens with an emphatic particle, breaks off before completing the sentence, and then starts again with a second emphatic particle. Arabic grammarians describe this as a resumption, and commentators read the interruption as itself meaningful: the promise is too urgent to wait for the grammar. Similar breaks appear at other high points in the Quran.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The promise is framed as a denial of loss rather than a description of gain, which fits how people actually worry. Nobody doubts that God can reward; what they doubt is whether the small, unwitnessed things register at all. The ayah answers that directly. It also shifts the qualifying description at the end from belief to good work, so the guarantee attaches to what was done rather than to a label held.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the guarantee and adds that the work of male and female counts alike.
Sets the smallest possible unit: an atom's weight of good or of evil is seen.
Later in the surah, a record that leaves out nothing small or large.

studies.applyIt: Think of one thing you do that nobody thanks you for and that would not be noticed if you stopped: a message you send weekly, a job at home, money that leaves your account. Do it again this week without mentioning it to anyone. This ayah is addressed precisely to the part of you that wonders whether it registers.

studies.title: The Things That Last
studies.meaning: Two things are named and neither is condemned. Wealth and children are called the ornament of this life, which grants that their attraction is real and located exactly where the surah placed it earlier. Set against them is a phrase left deliberately open: the lasting good things. The commentators offer a range for what it covers, from remembrance and prayer to any righteous act, and most decline to narrow it. The comparison is made twice, in reward and in hope.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The ayah follows the parable of the man with two gardens who told his companion he had more wealth and a stronger following, and whose gardens were destroyed overnight. It also follows the image of the world as vegetation that rain raises and wind scatters. The commentators report no specific occasion. Placing the ayah there makes it the conclusion of a story rather than a general maxim.

keyTerms.note: An active participle of remaining, in the feminine plural, with no noun attached. The absence is what makes the phrase famous: it names a category and leaves the reader to fill it.
From a root meaning to come back. The reward is described as something returning to the one who sent it out, which is a different picture from a prize handed over at the end.
The word for what a person leans forward towards. Saying the lasting things are better as hope means they are the better thing to want, which is a claim about the present rather than the future.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Wealth and sons were the two measures of a man in that society, and they were connected. Sons meant hands for the herd, riders in a feud, and someone to keep your name. A rich man with no sons was pitied; a poor man with many was still counted. Naming exactly those two as ornament was naming the whole scoring system the audience used on each other.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase about the lasting good things appears twice in the Quran, here and in another Meccan surah, both times in the same phrase and both times in a comparison. Reports from the companions attach it to particular phrases of remembrance, while many commentators keep it wide. Both readings have circulated side by side since the earliest period.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah does not ask anyone to stop valuing wealth or children. It ranks them, which is a different operation, and it ranks them by duration rather than by worth. That leaves ordinary attachments intact while removing their claim to be ultimate. The second comparison is the sharper one. Saying the lasting things are better as hope reaches into what a person spends the day wanting, which is harder to adjust than what they spend it doing.

crossReferences.why: The other occurrence of the same phrase, closing on return rather than on hope.
The parable this ayah concludes, about a man whose two gardens made him certain.
Lists the same attractions in more detail and calls them the enjoyment of this life.

studies.applyIt: Ask yourself what you hoped for when you woke up this morning. Not what you believe you should hope for: the actual first thought. Write it down in five words. Then leave the note somewhere you will see it in a week. This ayah compares two hopes rather than two possessions, and the comparison only works if you know what yours is.

studies.title: If The Ocean Were Ink
studies.meaning: The surah ends by placing three very different things side by side. First a garden described as hospitality, a word for what a host sets out on arrival, with no wish to be moved from it. Then an image of scale: the sea would run dry before the words of the Lord did, and another sea after it. Then a final instruction that reduces everything to two conditions, righteous work and worship with nothing else added underneath it.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, closing a surah that answered questions put by opponents to test the message. The classical sources report a specific occasion for the last ayah in some accounts, concerning a man who prayed and also wanted to be seen praying, though the reports differ and several commentators leave it general. The ayah about the sea is reported in connection with a question about how much knowledge had been given.

keyTerms.note: The word for what a host lays out for a guest on arrival, before the real hosting begins. Calling the garden that suggests it is the reception rather than the whole of what is coming.
From a root meaning to extend or supply, the same root as the word for reinforcement used two clauses later. The image and its answer are built from one root, which the translation cannot show.
The word for a person considered as flesh and skin, rather than the word that emphasises the human as a species or a soul. It is the plainest available term, which is the point of the sentence.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Ink was made from soot and gum and kept in small quantities, and writing was a specialist trade. A scribe measured his supply carefully, and running out mid-document was a real interruption. Setting the sea against an inkwell was not a poetic flourish to people who had watched one being refilled. The comparison worked because everyone knew how little ink a person actually had.
studies.didYouKnow: The surah opens with praise for a Book with no crookedness and closes by saying the words of the Lord would outlast the sea as ink. Its first and last movements are both about the extent of revelation. The word used for the garden here appears only twice in the Quran, and this is one of the two places.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The last ayah does two things at once. It denies the messenger any status beyond being human and receiving revelation, which removes him as an object of devotion in the same breath as it establishes his role. And it states the whole requirement in one sentence: do good work, and put nothing beside God in the worship of God. Everything the surah has narrated, the cave, the gardens, the journey, resolves into that.

crossReferences.why: Multiplies the same image: all the trees as pens and seven seas as ink.
The other place the same word for the garden appears, promised to the heirs.
Another place the messenger is told to say he is only a human being.

studies.applyIt: Take one thing you did this week for a good reason and ask what the second reason was. There usually is one, and it is usually about how it looked. Do not scold yourself. Just find the next occasion to do the same thing where nobody will know, and see whether you still want to. That is the test this ayah sets.
